text.en: In 1984 Rakesh Sharma, the first Indian astronaut in space, was asked by the Prime Minister how India looked from above. From that height India's mountains, rivers, deserts and coasts form one great picture. On the ground the same land is full of variety. In this chapter we travel across India's geography, from the Himalayas to the islands.

India and its neighbours Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka and Myanmar form the Indian Subcontinent, so called because it is a part of the continent of Asia. The Indian Ocean in the south and the Bay of Bengal in the east are natural boundaries, and mountains guard the north. The many colours on the physical map of India already show its geographical diversity: mountains, plains, plateaus, deserts, coasts and islands.
The Himalayas, about 2,500 km long, seem to touch the sky. They are the source of the Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra river systems, whose tributaries give water for drinking, farming and industry to hundreds of millions of people. Gaumukh, the edge of the Gangotri Glacier, is the source of the Ganga. Long ago India was part of a bigger landmass called Gondwana, next to Africa. India drifted northwards and collided with Asia; the rocks of the sea between them were folded upward to form the Himalayas. India is still pushing into Asia at about five centimetres each year. Ladakh is a cold desert, with unique wildlife such as snow leopards, ibex and Tibetan antelopes, and yaks are very important for people. The Great Himalayan National Park conserves mountain life.
The Northern Plains lie south of the Himalayas and are watered by a large number of rivers such as the Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra and their tributaries, which spread fertile soil rich in minerals. This makes the region highly fertile and ideal for agriculture and dense settlement. The Indian gharial, a fish-eating crocodile 2.5 to 4.5 m long, lives in these rivers. One river grows bigger in summer instead of drying up, because Himalayan snow melts and feeds it.
The Thar Desert is in western India. Sand dunes form when the wind shifts and shapes the sand into hills. People there even scour utensils with sand. The Aravalli Hills, among the oldest mountain ranges in the world, lie across Delhi, Rajasthan, Haryana and Gujarat. Historic forts such as Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh and Ranthambore are built there, and the hills were an excellent protection from enemies.
The Peninsular Plateau is an old and stable landmass. It tilts a little to the east, so rivers like the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri flow across it from west to east into the Bay of Bengal. The Western Ghats, declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site, are rich in forests and wildlife. Tribal communities live largely in parts of Jharkhand, West Bengal, Odisha, Assam, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Telangana and Gujarat.
The West Coast has beaches of golden sand and black rocks. Most rivers here begin in the Western Ghats, flow swiftly and form estuaries. The East Coast lies between the Eastern Ghats and the Bay of Bengal, from the Ganga delta to Kanyakumari. The Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri and Mahanadi make fertile deltas ideal for farming. Lakshadweep is an archipelago, a group of islands, in the Arabian Sea near Kerala. In the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Barren Island has the only active volcano in India. The Sundarbans in West Bengal, shared with Bangladesh, have one of the highest rainfalls in the world and are rich in forests, wildlife and fertile land.
This varied geography gave India different foods, crops, dresses and cultures, and rivers and mountains have been sacred to people everywhere. Our geography has helped unite people through shared rivers, trade and pilgrimage.

problem.en: Trace the Ganga from source to sea using the chapter.

text.en: It begins at Gaumukh, the edge of the Gangotri Glacier in the Himalayas.
It flows through the Northern Plains, bringing fertile soil.
It ends in the Ganga delta in the Bay of Bengal, near the Sundarbans.

problem.en: Why do the rivers of the Peninsular Plateau flow east?

text.en: The plateau tilts a little to the east.
So the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri flow towards the Bay of Bengal.
Rivers of the Western Ghats flow west because they begin close to the west coast.

prompt.en: Describe three of India's physical divisions and how they affect life.

requiredIdeas.en: Coasts and islands: trade, fishing, deltas.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking all of India is plains.
Mixing the East and West coasts.

points.en: India has mountains, plains, plateau, desert, coasts and islands.
The Himalayas formed when India drifted into Asia.
The Northern Plains are fertile; the plateau tilts east.
Geography unites India through rivers and shared culture.
